## Project milestones

- [Part 0: Team agreement + Collaboration in GitHub](#sec-collaboration): due Tuesday, September 29

- [Part 1: Project proposal](#sec-proposal): due Tuesday, September 29

- [Part 2: Exploratory data analysis](#sec-eda): due Thursday, October 29

- [[Part 3: Presentation + Presentation comments](#presentation)]{#sec-presentation}: Monday, November 23 in lab

- [Part 4: Draft report + Peer review](#sec-draft-report): Monday, November 30 in lab

- [Part 5: Final write up + Project repo](#sec-writeup): due Friday, December 4

## Introduction

The goal of the final project is for you to use regression to analyze data and explore a research question of your choice. The data may be from an existing data set or you may collect your own data from the internet.

Choose the data based on your group's interests or work you all have done in other courses or research projects. The goal of this project is for you to demonstrate proficiency in the techniques we have covered in this class (and beyond, if you like!) and apply them to a data set to analyze it in a meaningful way.

::: callout-important
**All analyses must be done in RStudio using Quarto and GitHub, and your analysis and written report must be reproducible.**

**All work for the project will be submitted in your project GitHub repo. There are no Gradescope submissions on the project.**
:::

### Logistics

You will complete the project as a lab team. The primary deliverables for the project are the following:

1.  An in-person presentation about the exploratory data analysis and initial modeling
2.  A reproducible final write up detailing your analysis and results
3.  A GitHub repository containing all work from the project --\>

There are intermediate milestones and peer review assignments throughout the semester to help you work towards the primary deliverables. These milestones are described below.

[Click here](https://prodduke-my.sharepoint.com/:x:/r/personal/mt324_duke_edu/Documents/STA%20221%20Lab%20Groups.xlsx?d=w5b50723cce064457b91bb28c55596f1a&csf=1&web=1&e=g5TNDT&nav=MTVfe0I0RDU4MzA5LTZERkMtNEM5MS04OUNFLTU2RUNFQzc3Qjc3OH0) to see your project teams.

Complete the team following before starting the project proposal:

✅ If you haven’t already, come up with a team name. You can’t use the same name as another team, so I encourage you to be creative! Your TA will get your team name by the end of lab.

✅ Fill out the team agreement. This will help you figure out a plan for communication, and working together during labs and outside of class. You can find the team agreement in the GitHub repo **team-agreement-\[github_team_name\]**.

When you are done typing, render and push all changes to GitHub. Then all team members, click **pull** to see the updated document in your RStudio container.

### Grading

This milestone is worth 5 points and will be graded based on completion.

## Part 1: Project proposal {#sec-proposal}

::: callout-important
## Submission

Write the narrative and analysis (Sections 1- 4) for each data set in `proposal.qmd`. Put the data set and the data dictionary in the \`data\` folder in the repo. Push the \`qmd\` and rendered \`pdf\` documents to GitHub by the deadline, **Tuesday, September 29 at 11:59pm.**
:::

The purpose of the project proposal is for your team to identify the data set you're interested in analyzing to investigate one of your potential research topics. **To do so, you will propose 2 - 3 data sets.** If you're unsure where to find data, you can use the list of potential data sources on the [Tips + resources](project-tips.html).

::: callout-important
You must use one of the proposed data sets for your final project, unless instructed otherwise in the teaching team feedback.
:::

Each data set must meet the following criteria:

- At least 500 observations
- At least 10 columns, such that at least 6 of the columns are useful and unique predictor variables.
  - e.g., identifier variables such as "name", "ID number", etc. are <u>not</u> useful predictor variables.

  - e.g., if you have multiple columns with the same information (e.g. "state abbreviation" and "state name"), then they are not unique predictors.
- At least one variable that can be identified as a reasonable response variable.
  - The response variable can be quantitative or categorical.
- A mix of quantitative and categorical variables that can be used as predictors.
- May not use a data set directly from lecture notes or assignments. If you use data from the same original data source (e.g., the lemurs data), you must add enough new variables and observations to make your data distinct from the data used in class.

::: callout-warning
### Types of data sets to avoid

- Data that are likely violate the independence condition. Therefore, avoid data with repeated measures, data collected over time, etc.

- Data sets in which there is no information about how the data were originally collected

- Data sets in which there are missing or unclear definitions about the observations and/or variables
:::

**Ask a member of the teaching team if you're unsure whether your data set meets the criteria.**

::: callout-tip
As you look for data sets, consider what topics your team is interested in or curious about. You can think about potential research questions you're interested in exploring first, then look for data sets that can help you answer those questions.

If you need help generating ideas, start by discussing the topics each of you put down as potential interest for the project in the Get to Know You Survey at the beginning of the semester.
:::

Include the following information for [**each**]{.underline} data set.

### Section 1: Data description

- The source of the data set, i.e., where you obtained the data.

- A description of when and how the data were originally collected (by the original data curator, not necessarily how you found the data)

- A description of the observations and general characteristics being measured

### Section 2: Research question

- A brief description of the topic that would be investigated with the data and your motivation for investigating this topic

- The potential audience(s) for your analysis, i.e., who might be most interested in this research? For example: policymakers, researchers, industry professionals, the general public, etc.

- One or two potential research questions you could analyze using this data set. *(Note: These are draft questions at this point. These questions may change in the next step of the project as you learn more about the data.)*

### Section 3: Variables

- Visualization of the proposed response variable.

- List of variables that will be considered as predictors

  - If there are more than 20 potential predictors, you can provide general descriptions of the types of variables that are considered as predictors (e.g., demographic variables)

### Section 4: Codebook

- Include a list of the variables in the data and their definitions.

  - You may directly use a codebook provided by the data source, as long as you cite it.

### AI Disclosure

Provide a brief description of how your team used AI (if at all) to complete this project milestone. If you used AI, include the name and version of the AI tool(s) used. If you did not use AI, you can state "We did not use AI to complete this milestone." *Note: AI use will not negatively affect your grade, provided it is accurately disclosed and in alignment with the course academic honesty policy.*

### Grading

The anticipated length is 1 - 2 pages per data set for Sections 1 - 4. The length of the codebook will vary based on the data set.

The proposal is worth 10 points and will be graded based on accurately and comprehensively addressing the criteria stated above. Points will be assigned based on a holistic review of the project proposal.

- **Excellent (9 - 10 pts) :** All required elements are completed and are accurate. There are at least two data sets that meet the requirements (or the team has otherwise discussed the data with Professor Tackett) and that do not pose obvious violations to the modeling assumptions. There is a thoughtful and comprehensive description of the data, potential research questions, visualization of the response variable, and potential predictors for at least two data sets. The narrative is written clearly, all tables and visualizations are nicely formatted, and the work would be presentable in a professional setting.

- **Strong (7 -8 pts):** Requirements are mostly met, but there are some elements that are incomplete or inaccurate. Some minor revision of the work required before team is ready for next project milestone.

- **Satisfactory (5 - 6 pts):** Requirements partially met, but there are some elements that are incomplete and/or inaccurate. Major revision of the work required before team is ready for next project milestone.

- **Needs Improvement (3 - 4pts):** Requirements are largely unmet, and there are major elements that are incomplete and/or inaccurate. Substantial revisions of the work required before team is ready for next project milestone.

## Project GitHub repo {#project-repo}

All written work (with exception of presentation slides) should be reproducible, and the GitHub repo should be neatly organized. =

The GitHub repo should have the following structure:

- `README`: Project title and team name updated, along with a short project summary

- `written-report.qmd` & `written-report.pdf` (or other format): Final written report

- `proposal.qmd` & `proposal.pdf`: Project proposal

- `/data`: Folder that contains the data set for the final project

- `/data/README.md`: Codebook and source for data set --\>

- `project.Rproj`: File specifying the RStudio project

- `/presentation`: Folder with the presentation slides or link to slides.

- `.gitignore`: File that lists all files that are in the local RStudio project but not the GitHub repo --\>

- Any other files should be neatly organized into clearly labeled folders.

Update the README of the project repo with your project title, short summary, and team members' names.

Points for reproducibility + organization will be based on the reproducibility of the written report and the organization of the project GitHub repo. The repo should be neatly organized as described above, there should be no extraneous files, and all text in the `README` should be easily readable.

There is no late work accepted on the draft report or presentation. Other components of the project may be accepted up to 48 hours late. A 10% late deduction will apply for each 24-hour period late. The submission time is based on the commits in your GitHub repo.

**Be sure to turn in your work early to avoid any technological mishaps.**
